title: Authentication and Authorization Basics
description: Understand the fundamental difference between authentication (who you are) and authorization (what you can do), and learn how ASP.NET Core's built-in security system handles both.

blocks.text: Security in web applications comes down to two distinct questions: Who are you? and What are you allowed to do? Authentication answers the first question by verifying identity. Authorization answers the second by controlling access to resources.

Think of it like a hotel. Authentication is the front desk checking your ID and issuing a key card. Authorization is the key card determining which rooms you can unlock. Both are necessary — knowing who someone is does not automatically grant them access to everything.

blocks.title: Important: Authentication always comes first
blocks.text: ASP.NET Core processes authentication before authorization. The authentication system determines the user's identity, and the authorization system checks what that identity is permitted to do. Never swap this order — authorization depends on authentication having already run.

When a user logs into an application, they provide credentials — typically a username and password. The authentication system validates these credentials against a user store. If valid, it issues a token or cookie that represents the user's identity. Every subsequent request includes this token, allowing the application to recognize the user without asking for credentials again.

ASP.NET Core supports multiple authentication methods called schemes. The most common are cookie authentication for browser-based applications and JWT bearer authentication for APIs. You can configure multiple schemes and choose which one to use per endpoint.

blocks.title: Common authentication schemes
items: Cookie authentication — Stores identity in an encrypted HTTP cookie for browser-based apps
JWT Bearer — Uses signed JSON Web Tokens sent in the Authorization header for APIs
OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect — Delegates authentication to external providers like Google or Microsoft
API Key — Simple key-based authentication for machine-to-machine communication

blocks.text: Authorization determines whether an authenticated user can access a specific resource or perform a specific action. ASP.NET Core provides a policy-based authorization system that evaluates rules defined in code. These rules can check roles, claims, or custom requirements.

The simplest form of authorization is role-based: users in the 'Admin' role can access admin pages, while regular users cannot. More advanced scenarios use policies that combine multiple requirements, such as requiring both a specific role and a minimum age claim.

blocks.title: Cookie authentication configuration
blocks.content: Configuring cookie authentication with login and access denied paths.

blocks.text: In this configuration, CookieAuthenticationDefaults.AuthenticationScheme sets 'Cookies' as the default scheme. When a user visits a protected page without being logged in, ASP.NET Core redirects them to '/Account/Login'. After a successful login, a cookie is issued that authenticates subsequent requests automatically.

The [Authorize] attribute is the most common way to enforce authorization in controllers and Razor Pages. When applied to a controller or action, it requires the user to be authenticated. You can add parameters to restrict access to specific roles, policies, or authentication schemes.

blocks.title: Using the [Authorize] attribute
blocks.content: Different ways to apply authorization at the controller and action level.

blocks.text: The [AllowAnonymous] attribute overrides [Authorize] on the same action or controller. This is useful when a controller is generally protected but has a few public endpoints like a product listing page.

blocks.title: Tip: Global authorization policy
blocks.text: You can make [Authorize] the default for all controllers by adding a global authorization filter in Program.cs: options.Filters.Add(new AuthorizeFilter()). Use [AllowAnonymous] to opt out for specific actions.

Modern ASP.NET Core identity systems are built around claims. A claim is a statement about a user, such as 'email is user@example.com' or 'role is Admin'. The user's identity is a collection of claims issued during authentication.

Claims are flexible because they are not limited to a fixed schema. A user can have claims for their department, clearance level, subscription tier, or any other attribute your application needs. Authorization policies evaluate these claims to make access decisions.

terms.definition: The process of verifying a user's identity, typically through credentials like username/password, tokens, or external providers.
The process of determining whether an authenticated user has permission to access a resource or perform an action.
Statements about a user such as name, email, or role. The user's identity is a collection of claims.
A named configuration that defines how authentication is performed, such as 'Cookies' or 'JwtBearer'.
An attribute applied to controllers or actions that requires the user to meet specific authentication or authorization requirements.

blocks.title: Configure Cookie Authentication
blocks.description: Set up cookie authentication in an ASP.NET Core MVC application, protect a controller with [Authorize], and test the login flow.
steps: Create a new MVC project: 'dotnet new mvc -n AuthBasicsDemo'
In Program.cs, add AddAuthentication with CookieAuthenticationDefaults.AuthenticationScheme and configure LoginPath and AccessDeniedPath
Add app.UseAuthentication() and app.UseAuthorization() to the pipeline
Create an AccountController with Login and Logout actions
In the Login GET action, return a simple login view with email and password fields
In the Login POST action, validate the credentials (for testing, accept any non-empty values), call SignInAsync, and redirect to the home page
Add [Authorize] to a DashboardController and verify that unauthenticated users are redirected to login
blocks.expectedOutcome: Visiting /Dashboard without logging in redirects to /Account/Login. After submitting the login form, the user is authenticated and can access the dashboard. Logging out clears the authentication cookie and redirects to the home page.

items.text: I can explain the difference between authentication and authorization
items.hint: Authentication verifies identity; authorization controls access.

items.text: I understand why UseAuthentication must come before UseAuthorization
items.hint: Authorization needs the user's identity to be established first.

items.text: I can configure cookie authentication in Program.cs
items.hint: Use AddCookie with LoginPath and AccessDeniedPath options.

items.text: I can apply [Authorize] to protect controllers and actions
items.hint: Apply [Authorize] at the controller level for full protection.

items.text: I understand what claims are and how they represent user identity
items.hint: Claims are key-value pairs describing the user, like email and role.

items.text: I can read user claims in a controller using User.FindFirst
items.hint: Use ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier for the user ID and ClaimTypes.Email for the email.

blocks.title: Authentication and Authorization Summary
points: Authentication verifies identity; authorization controls access to resources
Cookie authentication stores identity in encrypted HTTP cookies for browser apps
JWT bearer authentication uses tokens in the Authorization header for APIs
UseAuthentication must always be registered before UseAuthorization in the pipeline
[Authorize] protects controllers and actions; [AllowAnonymous] overrides it
Claims are the building blocks of identity in ASP.NET Core, representing user attributes
blocks.takeaway: Understanding the distinction between authentication and authorization is fundamental to building secure applications. ASP.NET Core provides a unified, policy-based system that handles both concerns with minimal boilerplate.
